title: Monroe coach, community mentor back East football players to get chance to play Saturday - 13WHAM-TV
content: Why is Rochester City School District challenging disqualifications? Rochester, N.Y. (WHAM) — A Monroe High School assistant coach and a Rochester community mentor are urging the community to support the student-athletes involved in a fight after Saturday’s East High–Monroe football game. They also want East players who were not involved to have the chance to play in the Section V championship game this Saturday. Section V is reviewing the incident and the student-athletes involved. The Rochester City School District says it is working with Section V and the New York State Public High School Athletic Association to challenge disqualifications for East players it believes were misidentified. Greg Hopkins, an assistant coach for Monroe and founder and director of Changing the Community, said the incident does not reflect the football program or the young people involved. “It was terrible, honestly, because that’s not what the program is, not who the kids are, that’s not what the community is,” Hopkins said. He described the altercation as a disagreement among “brothers” that spilled beyond the game. BACKGROUND:  Section V, RCSD reviewing end-of-game brawl between Monroe, East High football teams Hopkins said most of the players were not involved in the fight and were trying to break it up. He estimated about 10 of roughly 80 players were involved. “It wasn’t everybody,” he said. “It’s like 80 kids on, 40 kids on both sides. We had about 10 kids getting into it. That’s another 70 kids just looking to break it up.” Hopkins said he has worked with players from both schools through Changing the Community, and described them as “my kids.” He said he wants the East players who were not involved to be able to continue their season. “The kids that had the altercations, that did things they weren’t supposed to do, I’m sure they’re going to feel bad they can’t play next week,” Hopkins said. “And the kids that didn’t do nothing, which was, again, the majority of the kids, don’t need to be punished for something they earned and worked for.” The East players helped end Monroe’s 20-game winning streak, Hopkins said, and should have the opportunity to compete for a championship. Bilel Smith, a community member and founder of Black Dads Matter, said the incident should not define the teams or the young people involved. “I really hope that this community can wrap its arms around these young men as opposed to condemning them,” Smith said. Smith said players from East and Monroe have built relationships across the community, including through Changing the Community. He said both teams have raised the level of high school football in the Rochester City School District and called for the community to support them. “The way to erase the memory of this isn’t by not playing,” Smith said. “It’s by making sure we give them an opportunity to show who they really are.” The Rochester City School District released the following statement from Superintendent Dr. Eric Jay Rosser:

title: Mums v Big Pharma review – the ‘bored, hysterical housewives’ who exposed a horrifying scandal - The Guardian
content: Janet Williams and Emma Murphy both had children with disabilities, then started doing some digging … and uncovered a jaw-dropping medical fiasco that rivals thalidomide. Long may they fight! Tales of corporate or governmental wrongdoing are often hugely complicated. Documents destroyed, witnesses untraceable, endless obfuscations and legal intricacies invoked. If the people doing the uncovering are ordinary folk, unarmed with fancy lawyers or untrained in the ways of big business or statecraft, the story often becomes even more of a switchback ride before the mind-boggling whole is laid bare. Just occasionally, however, the story is very simple (though no less mind-boggling). Such a case is that of the sodium valproate scandal, uncovered thanks to a campaign that was started 17 years ago by two mothers who began to suspect that their children’s disabilities had a specific cause. Janet Williams had two sons with developmental delays. For years she was told by doctors that there was nothing wrong: “You truly believed that if there was something wrong or something that needed explanation, they would tell you,” she says now, remembering her naive younger self and her trust in the medical profession. Then, in 2009, the boys were referred to a specialist who almost casually informed her that their condition was probably a result of her epilepsy medication, Epilim. It was the brand name for sodium valproate, discovered in 1962 to be an effective anti-seizure drug, and also used to treat bipolar disorder. By the time Williams was having her children in the 1990s, it was one of the most widely prescribed treatments for epilepsy in the UK. Williams started distributing leaflets in her home town of Pilling, Lancashire, telling her story and asking other potentially afflicted families to get in touch. They did. They had questions she couldn’t answer, so she started researching everything she could at Manchester Central library. Then she made the news and Emma Murphy from nearby Bury, five of whose children (out of six) had similar difficulties to Williams’s after exposure to Epilim, got in touch. To Murphy’s continuing amusement – “I’d just been reading women’s magazines and sitting at home watching Coronation Street!” – they began putting together evidence that would eventually reveal a scandal to rival thalidomide in scale and suffering. Alongside the mothers’ story runs that of Prof Jill Clayton-Smith, a clinical geneticist working in Manchester in the mid-90s, who began to notice a recurring cluster of features among the children born to women treated for epilepsy. She investigated further and presented her findings – including a 1984 US paper describing “foetal valproate syndrome” – at a conference. “It wasn’t received as well as I’d hoped,” she says delicately. The male-dominated audience essentially scoffed at her “anecdotal” data and ignored it. Prof David Chadwick, however, encouraged her to embark on a formal study that could not be refuted. Williams’s children would become part of it and it would eventually help determine that sodium valproate carries a 10% risk of causing physical malformations and a 30-40% risk of causing serious neurodevelopmental disorders in those exposed. The drug is estimated to have affected 39,399 babies since the risk was first identified. In 2011, Murphy, Williams and 138 other families were undertaking a class action suit against the drug manufacturer Sanofi Aventis. Excitement and hope were building when suddenly their legal aid was withdrawn after they were deemed unlikely to succeed, and lawyers formally discontinued action. By 2013 they had regrouped and began investigating the apparent regulatory failure in licensing the drug for use by women of childbearing age. They had several futile meetings in Westminster. “We were referred to as ‘bored, hysterical housewives’,” says Murphy. Williams remembers an official turning to her to ask if she understood what a word meant. She did. “The way they dealt with us was sickening … But it drove me on.” They started secretly recording the meetings. We hear audio of someone saying: “The neurologists weren’t in favour of having this acknowledgment of risk … Doctors don’t like being told what to do,” and suggesting that patient warnings on packaging weren’t necessary because people could find the information on the internet if they wanted – “Your Facebook site’s great!” “The ignorance,” says Williams. “The arrogance.” “Bastards,” murmurs Murphy. The thalidomide campaign team advised them to go to the National Archives at Kew and look for the meeting notes from the Committee on Safety of Medicines (CSM) when the drug came on the market. In 2015 they found the smoking gun: the CSM’s response to Sanofi’s statement to them that the drug was harmful to foetuses. To warn about this, it said, would cause women “fruitless anxiety.” So nobody was told anything. This is where medical misogyny, a cancer in the system that corrupts everything it touches, inexorably leads. There was a government review, there was handwringing, there was the promise two years ago of state compensation. There have been no payments yet to the estimated 20,000 families affected by the drug. But bored, hysterical housewives never give up. God bless them, and damn the rest. Mums v Big Pharma aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer The Guardian has something US newsrooms don’t: guaranteed independence. title: Westridge School Wins CIF-Southern Section Division V Volleyball Championship - Pasadena Now
content:
Westridge School’s varsity girls volleyball team captured the CIF-Southern Section Division V championship Friday, November 6, defeating El Toro High School (Orange County, CA), 3-2, in a thrilling five-set match at Cerritos College in Norwalk. The Tigers secured the title in a hard-fought finale, winning the deciding set 15-13 after rallying from an 8-11 deficit. The victory marked Westridge’s first CIF-Southern Section volleyball championship since 2006. Junior Bennett Thein led the Tigers’ offensive effort with a match-high 35 kills, while Misk Youssef added 14 and Chloe Sim contributed 10. Freshman Jolene Lee delivered a crucial service ace to bring Westridge to match point before an El Toro error ended the contest. The championship capped an impressive postseason run that included victories over Viewpoint, Irvine, and La Serna before the Tigers advanced to the finals. Westridge now moves on to the CIF Southern California Regional playoffs, continuing its pursuit of a state championship. title: Formula V Line Air Power G10 PC Case (Review) - Poc Network // Tech
content:
In our first hands-on with the company Formula V Line, we get to discuss the new Air Power G10 PC Case. It is a mid-tower ATX chassis that is capable of redirecting its intake airflow right where your hardware needs it most, all without asking you to spend a premium on your case (which is ever so important in a time filled with tech inflation). BuildCustom PCs If the Formula V Line name is new to you, that’s because it is new to the U.S. The Taiwan-based PC hardware and gaming lifestyle brand has been building cases, cooling, power supplies, and even gaming chairs for enthusiasts overseas, and the Air Power G10 is the company’s first case in the U.S. market, and its official entry into the U.S. PC hardware space. It was first previewed at Computex 2026 and is now available through Newegg as well as other online retailers, which makes it easy to find without having to import anything. BuildCustom PCs The G10 comes in six finishes: Black, Black Rose Gold, Black Wood, White, Black Titanium Silver, and Black Dark Blue. The one we are looking at here is the standard Black, which is also one of the lower-priced options at $89.99. With a headline feature that is more than a gimmick, four included fans, and a layout that’s built around making upgrades less painful, it’s an interesting first impression for a brand most American builders haven’t had the chance to try. Let’s start with the look. The Air Power G10 is a steel-bodied mid-tower with a plastic front panel, and in Black it goes for a clean, minimalist, understated look rather than a loud gamer aesthetic. Overall, it measures 235 x 500 x 489mm, which is a fairly standard size for a modern ATX tower, and it supports ATX, Micro-ATX, and ITX motherboards with seven expansion slots. The other five finishes get a bit more adventurous, with metallic paint accents in Rose Gold and Titanium Silver, a wood-grain option, a dark blue, and a white, so if you want something with more personality, the lineup has options. The black version, though, is the one that fits in just about anywhere, and a plain black case is easy to build around. The front panel I/O is modern and sensible. You get one USB 3.2 Type-C port, two USB 3.0 ports, and HD audio, which is what we’d expect to see at this price. It’s worth noting that Formula V Line has also made the 3D design files for the fan grille panel available as a download, so anyone with a 3D printer can design and print their own custom panel. It’s a small touch, but it’s a nice nod to the DIY crowd. The real headline feature is the front intake. Rather than mounting the three front fans flat against the chassis, the G10 uses a two-step adjustable system where each fan sits on its own bracket and can be set to either 0° or 10°. That means you can aim each fan’s airflow slightly upward or downward, directing cool air toward the CPU area, the GPU, or splitting the difference by pointing one fan one way and the other two another. Each fan assembly can also be removed independently, making cleaning and replacement a lot easier than wrestling with a fixed front panel. A 10-degree change is not a dramatic redirect, and this isn’t going to transform a poorly planned build. What it does is give you a simple, tool-free way to fine-tune where your intake air goes, which, in a case designed around airflow, is a genuinely useful option to have. The adjustments have positive, defined stops, so it’s not a vague or fiddly mechanism, either. For cooling, the G10 is very well equipped. Out of the box you get four 120mm PA2 120 fans, three on the front intake and one on the rear exhaust, all featuring 4-pin PWM control and 3-pin ARGB lighting. That’s a better-than-expected starting point for under $100, and it means you can get a build up and running with real airflow from the start. From there, the case supports up to eleven 120mm fan positions in total: Those side and bottom positions are the ones to pay attention to, because most cases in this price range don’t offer them. Adding fans on the side to push air directly at the GPU, or on the bottom to feed the lower chamber, gives you a lot of room to design a cooling setup around your hardware rather than the other way around. Keep in mind that you’ll be shopping for seven additional fans to fill every slot, and with that many, you’ll want to plan for fan splitters or a hub to keep the cabling manageable. If you prefer liquid cooling, the G10 supports 240mm or 360mm radiators mounted at the top of the case. That covers the most popular AIO sizes for modern CPUs, including the 360mm class that most high-end builds use. It’s worth noting that the top is the only listed radiator mounting location, so if you were hoping to mount a radiator on the front or rear, this isn’t the case for that. Air coolers are supported as well, with up to 182mm of CPU cooler clearance, which is more than reasonable. This means, in many cases, you can  make use of the popular Noctua NH-D15 G2 or Noctua NH-D15 classic if you want to balance quiet with the ultimate fan/heatsink combo. Dust protection is handled by filters on the front, top, and bottom of the case, which cover the main intake and exhaust areas where dust is most likely to get in. With a design that encourages adding more fans, having filters in these locations means you’re not creating more places for dust to build up inside the system. The filters make routine cleaning a quick task, and combined with the removable front fan assemblies, keeping the case clean over the long run should be straightforward. This is a popular practice by most major case manufacturers. This is where the G10 does a lot of its quiet work. The lower chamber is modular, so the power supply and the lower fan bracket can swap between the front and rear positions. That means you can choose the bottom layout that suits your hardware, whether you want to prioritize cable routing, PSU placement, or the lower fan locations. The fan bracket is also removable, which makes installing fans, or working around a larger power supply (up to 160mm), a lot less frustrating. The rest of the case follows the same philosophy. Panels use a tool-free quick-release mechanism, so getting inside takes seconds rather than a handful of screws. Storage supports one 3.5-inch drive at the bottom and two 2.5-inch drives on the side (rear side of the motherboard), using a quick-release bracket for easy installation. A built-in GPU support bracket helps balance the weight of heavier graphics cards and can be adjusted vertically to match the thickness of the card. And GPU clearance tops out at an impressive 420mm, so even the longest modern graphics cards should fit without trouble. A case review ultimately comes down to one question: how well does it keep your hardware cool? We approached the G10 with that in mind, focusing on the kinds of heavy builds where thermals really matter, such as a high-wattage GPU paired with a hot-running CPU. The G10’s airflow layout is built for exactly that kind of system. With three fans pulling air in from the front and the ability to tilt them toward the components that need it, the case has a clear path for cool air to travel from front to back, with the rear fan and a top-mounted radiator or fans taking care of the exhaust. In a typical high-end build, a 360mm AIO mounted at the top acting as exhaust, three front intake fans, and a rear exhaust fan make for a balanced setup that should keep both CPU and GPU temperatures well managed. Adding side or bottom fans to feed a large graphics card is where the case really opens up for the hottest builds, and that’s something many cases in this price range simply can’t do. The tilt feature is useful, but it’s best thought of as fine-tuning, not a game changer. Pointing the front fans down toward a power-hungry GPU or up toward the CPU cooler is a smart way to put air where it’s needed, especially in builds with a large graphics card in the lower half of the case, but the difference is going to be measured in a few degrees rather than a dramatic drop. The real benefit comes from the combination of tilting intake, the sheer number of fan positions, and the flexibility to change the layout of the lower chamber. That, and the pattern you take for balancing the overall air that is coming in or out of the case (fan directions). Builders who enjoy tweaking will love it. There are some things to keep in mind. A heavy build that fills the case with a long GPU, a 360mm radiator, and several drives is going to be a tighter fit than a lighter one, so a bit of planning on component placement goes a long way. The stock four fans are a great start, but the best thermal results will come from adding more, and that adds cost and cable management work (like with any case). On the usability side, building in the G10 is a pleasant experience. The tool-free panels, removable fan bracket, and swappable PSU layout all make it easy to get components in and out, and the adjustable GPU bracket is a thoughtful addition that helps reduce the strain on the PCIe slot from heavy graphics cards. Taking everything together, the G10 punches above its price. The airflow design is smart, the fan count and layout are generous, and the modular approach makes building and upgrading easier. The tilt mechanism is more of a refinement than a revolution, and the radiator support is limited to the top, but these are minor points for a case that gets so many of the fundamentals right. At $89.99 for the black version (the White, Titanium Silver, and Dark Blue models are $99.99), the G10 is priced very competitively for what’s included. Four fans, a unique front airflow design, a modular PSU chamber, and support for 360mm radiators and 420mm GPUs are typically features that we see on more expensive cases. Formular V Line seems to be hitting the market swinging. The Formula V Line Air Power G10 is an impressive first case for the U.S. market. It starts with a clever idea in the tilting front intake fans, then backs it up with the things that actually matter to builders: four included PWM/ARGB fans, support for up to 11 x 120mm fans, a 360mm top radiator, 420mm of GPU clearance, filters on the front, top, and bottom, and a modular lower chamber that gives you real choices in how you lay out your build. All of that at $89.99 for the Black version is a very strong value. It isn’t perfect. The tilt range is modest, radiators are limited to the top of the case, and filling all of those fan slots is going to take additional fans and a bit of cable wrangling. As a new brand in the U.S., it also still needs time to build a track record. But for anyone putting together a high-performance system with a hot GPU or a high-end CPU and doesn’t want to spend a fortune on the case, the Air Power G10 deserves a spot on the shortlist. As I said, the company looks like it is hitting the market swinging, and isn’t playing around. You can find it at Newegg, as well as other online retailers, and with six finishes to choose from, there’s a version to match just about any build. *Average price is based on the time this article was published Are you a manufacturer or distributor that would like us to test something out for review? title: Down Volume V: Release Date, King Diamond & What We Know - 25YearsLaterSite.com
content: Down, the New Orleans sludge metal supergroup, release Volume V on November 20 via Nuclear Blast Records. Here’s what “Blood Oath,” “The Myth” and the songs for King Diamond and Ozzy Osbourne tell us before the full album arrives. New Orleans sludge metal supergroup Down will release Volume V on November 20, 2026, via Nuclear Blast Records. Per Consequence (August 2026), lead single “Blood Oath” arrived with the album’s announcement on August 19. “The Myth” followed with a music video, according to The Sound 228 (October 2026). Those two songs are all anyone outside the band has heard, me included. So this is a news piece, and our full review of the heavy metal record comes after release. A content note before you press play: Down’s music and interviews include explicit language. The title is a piece of arithmetic. Loaded Radio (August 2026) notes that Volume V is Down’s first full-length since Down III: Over the Under in 2007. The “fifth volume” count only works if the two Down IV EPs share one installment. Other outlets measure the gap from a different starting point. The MetalList (November 3, 2026) calls it the band’s first studio release since 2014’s Down IV – Part II EP. Loaded Radio is counting albums, and The MetalList is counting new music. Both are right. Both describe a long silence. Down has always run on its own clock. NOLA arrived in 1995, per The Sound 228 (October 2026). Now the back catalog is moving again, with Bandcamp listing a June 2026 remaster of Over the Under. For more on the singer’s other band, read our look at Phil Anselmo’s Pantera years. Kirk Windstein has set the bar himself. He compared the band’s current chemistry to NOLA, with 35 more years of songwriting experience behind it. Both Consequence (August 2026) and The Sound 228 (October 2026) carried the comparison. That is a bold standard for a fifth record. Invoking the debut tells you what the band thinks it has made. The process backs up that nostalgia. The MetalList (August 2026) reports two writing sessions at Anselmo’s home studio, Nodferatu’s Lair. The band has gone there to write since Down II, per The MetalList (August 2026). Per the same report, Pepper Keenan and Windstein tracked their guitars at the same time. That detail matters for a band built on two guitarists leaning into the same riff. Recording together keeps the push and pull of a live room. The official album announcement credits Eddie Mapp as producer alongside the band. Dave Fortman mixed the record, and Maor Appelbaum mastered it. The early results sound local. Consequence (August 2026) called “Blood Oath” a “doom grinder” built on a riff of “pure New Orleans sludge.” Anselmo says, per Theprp (August 2026), that the song carries New Orleans references locals will catch. The ten-song tracklist opens with “The Myth,” “Merciful Fate,” “Turn Out the Light,” “The Message,” and “Causeway Grief.” The back half runs “Blood Oath,” “They Walk the Night,” “They Came From Dust,” “Ozz,” and “Twice-Told Tales.” Two titles point outward, at the people who shaped this band. “Merciful Fate” sets King Diamond in a vocal duel with Anselmo, per the band’s August 2026 announcement. His wife, Livia Zita, adds harmony vocals, per The MetalList (November 3, 2026). The pun on Mercyful Fate, King Diamond’s old band, is hard to miss. Anselmo’s explanation is gentler than the joke. The MetalList (November 3, 2026), citing Fistful of Metal magazine, reports that the title came by accident during demos. Anselmo says it stuck because of the idea of a peaceful death. He also says he has known King “for a long, long time.” “Ozz” honors Ozzy Osbourne, according to Consequence (August 2026). We’ve also written about Pantera’s The Great Southern Trendkill. Here Anselmo and his bandmates pay respect to the singers who came before them. Put those two songs beside a title like “Causeway Grief” and a pattern appears. On paper, Volume V is a record about lineage and mortality, made by a band of lifers. I can’t yet say whether the music carries that weight. The tracklist suggests the band means it to. I care about this one because Down has always sounded personal. Its members come back to it when they have something to say. Twelve years after the last EP, a song about a peaceful death and a song for Ozzy suggest they do. “Blood Oath” and “The Myth” are promising, and Windstein’s NOLA comparison raises the stakes. Two songs can’t tell you how an album holds together, though. We’ll review Volume V in full when it lands on November 20. Highlights, deep dives and new obsessions without the spam.

title: Getting Ready: Lívia at the LACMA Gala - V Magazine
content: What does it really take to get gala-ready? Lívia takes V for a closer look at the magic and meticulous moments behind the gala look What does it really take to get gala-ready? Lívia takes V for a closer look at the magic and meticulous moments behind the gala look Lívia Nunes Marques might just be the coolest girl in town. The cultural trailblazer—known simply as Lívia—has collaborated with fashion heavyweights Dior, Miu Miu, and Prada, and now she’s touched down in Los Angeles for one of the fashion calendar’s most glamorous nights: the LACMA Gala. From the outside, getting ready for a night like this might look effortless. title: What Caleb Williams Told 10-Year-Old Podcasters Jimmy V and Hen Dawg at Their First Bears Game - TODAY.com
content: Last Chance! Score Tickets for Shop TODAY Holiday House What Caleb Williams Told 10-Year-Old Podcasters Jimmy V and Hen Dawg at Their First Bears Game It was a dream come true for viral kid podcasters Jimmy V and Hen-Dawg, who got to meet Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams before and after his team hosted the Tampa Bay Buccaneers Nov. 8 on “Sunday Night Football.” The 10-year-old kids, whose names are Henry “Hen-Dawg” Zotti and Jimmy “V” Maley, are huge Bears fans who were surprised with tickets to the game on TODAY on Nov. 4. Before the game, they got to walk around Soldier Field with Kaylee Hartung, who surprised them by saying they would head to the field where they walked by an end zone and sat on the “Football Night in America” set. Then, they chatted up Bears kicker Cairo Santos, before the main event: meeting Williams, which they said was their big goal. “Good to see y’all,” Williams said as he signed autographs for them. “Are you going to lock in?” Hen-Dawg asked, prompting Williams, who was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, to chuckle. “Are we your favorite podcasters?” Hen-Dawg then asked. “Y’all are. I gotta get back to work now,” he said before giving both boys a fist bump. Come game time, the pair was focused on rooting for the Bears. The Chicago team shook off four interceptions by Williams to win its fourth straight game on the strength of Santos’ walkoff field game to propel them to a 27-24 victory and improve their record to 7-2. The duo then reconnected with Williams after the game. “I’m happy y’all could make it,” he told them while signing more autographs. “We got a win for you.” Jimmy V and Hen-Dawg weren’t quite done yet, either, as they appeared live Nov. 9 on TODAY. For Hen-Dawg, there was no doubt what his favorite part of the night was. “Meeting Caleb Williams and going on the field at the end of the game,” he said. Hartun reminded the boys that Williams had told them their podcast was his favorite. “Yup,” Jimmy V said simply, while Hen-Dawg later confirmed that Williams did tell them that after the game. “I’m sure somebody has it on clip,” Jimmy V said about the moment where Williams told them. While the boys appeared to have a blast, they did have a difference of opinion over one matter: food. “I had two cheeseburgers, and they were massive, but they were so good,” Jimmy V said, noting the food was “perfect.” Hen-Dawg said he ate the same thing, “but I didn’t really like it that much.” The boys will have a chance to cool off for awhile before returning to gameday mode, as the Bears are on a bye week coming up and don’t play again until they host the New Orleans Saints on Nov. 22. title: UUC v. Repsol-YPF: the Supreme Court Ruling and Antitrust Damages in Argentina - Wolters Kluwer
content: UUC v. Repsol-YPF: the Supreme Court Ruling and Antitrust Damages in Argentina On 29 October 2026 the Argentine Supreme Court (CSJN) dismissed, for lack of standing of the plaintiff, the only collective follow-on damages action ever brought in Argentina, which had moreover obtained a judgment in its favour at two levels of jurisdiction. It did so twenty-four years after the claim was filed, by referring, “for the sake of brevity”, to the opinion issued by the Attorney General's Office in April 2023. In 2002 the consumer association Unión de Usuarios y Consumidores claimed the overcharge YPF had applied to LPG in the domestic market between 1993 and 1999. The conduct had been sanctioned as an abuse of dominance by Resolution SICyM 189/99, upheld by the Supreme Court in Fallos: 325:1702. The Federal Court of Appeals of La Plata (Chamber I) granted the claim and set direct damages at ARS 95,775,681 (1993/1997) and ARS 78,050,000 (1997/1999), finding, on the basis of expert evidence, that the overcharge had been passed on in full to final consumers. Since individual restitution was impossible, the first-instance court had ordered the defendant to fund the expansion of the natural gas network in low-income areas. The opinion, and with it the Court, rests on three grounds: The class is undefined: consumers scattered across the country over seven years, with no characterisation that would allow its members to be identified (Halabi, recital 20; Fallos: 338:1492). There are no homogeneous individual interests: YPF sold in the wholesale market, and LPG reached consumers through bottlers, distributors and retailers with different pricing strategies; moreover, YPF was not the only supplier. This follows Loma Negra (Fallos: 338:40). The remedy does not benefit the class: the gas network works would favour third parties, not those who paid the overcharge. The Court did not rule on limitation, on the effect of the final administrative sanction, on passing-on or on quantification. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs under Article 55 of Law 24,240 (Consumer Protection Law). The ruling consolidates the Loma Negra rule, now for unilateral conduct and an already quantified award: where there are intermediaries between the infringer and the final consumer, a consumer collective action fails the homogeneity test. In practice, this produces, through procedural means, an effect equivalent to Illinois Brick: the indirect purchaser is excluded even where it has been proven to have borne 100% of the overcharge. The difference from the US model is decisive. There, the exclusion of indirect purchasers is offset by the direct purchaser's full standing to recover the entire overcharge, plus treble damages. Here, the direct purchaser (the bottler) may sue, but the expert evidence itself states that it passed everything on, which exposes its claim to a passing-on defence. The likely outcome is that nobody recovers and the infringer keeps a rent of roughly ARS 174 million in 1990s pesos. The practical impact goes beyond that of an isolated precedent: On collective redress: in markets with a distribution chain (fuels, inputs, food, pharmaceuticals), which account for most cartel and abuse cases, consumer actions are effectively closed off. On deterrence: private enforcement ceases to complement administrative fines precisely where harm is most dispersed and individual actions are unviable. On Law 27,442: the case was decided under Laws 22,262 and 25,156, but the criterion is procedural and constitutional (Art. 43 of the National Constitution and Halabi), so it extends to the current regime. The current law has resolved much of what was litigated in UUC: the Tribunal's final decision is res judicata, and the civil judge must base the ruling on the facts and legal characterisation established in it (Art. 63); damages actions are time-barred after three years, or two years from the sanction becoming final (Art. 72), and limitation is suspended during the administrative proceedings (Art. 73). What it did not resolve is who may bring collective claims, since Article 62 refers to the general law. The ruling fills that gap restrictively, even though Article 65 recognises “direct and indirect” purchasers as injured parties. The ruling has real merits, particularly in upholding the compensatory nature of the action. Compensation is not redistribution. Rejecting an award that funds gas works for third parties reaffirms that damage must be compensated to those who suffered it. A cy-près remedy detached from the class turns a damages action into public policy decided by a judge. Requirement of class definition. Requiring the class to be identifiable from the outset protects the defendant's due process and delimits the scope of res judicata, in line with Halabi and subsequent case law (Fallos: 339:1077; 343:637). Risk of double recovery. Taking the distribution chain into account prevents the same overcharge from being recovered twice: by the bottler in its individual action and by consumers in the collective one. Each party bears its own costs. Applying Article 55 of Law 24,240 prevents the defeat from deterring the associations that bring these actions. No res judicata on the merits. Since the dismissal rests on standing, it should not bar individual claims, although at this stage limitation makes them illusory. The central problem is that the Court decided an admissibility issue at the end of the proceedings, without reasons of its own, and conflated standing with the merits. Referral in a 24-year case. Referring “for the sake of brevity” to a 2023 opinion in the country's most significant antitrust damages case is a missed opportunity. No guidance was given on limitation (Art. 54 of Law 25,156 versus the two-year term; now Arts. 72 and 73 of Law 27,442 for new cases), on the dies a quo, on the effect of the final administrative sanction, on passing-on or on quantification. The timing of the review. The opinion itself states that the class must be verified “at the initial stage of the proceedings”. Declaring it undefined after economic and accounting expert reports and two judgments is wasteful, and shifts onto the victims a failure that belongs to the procedural system. The reasonable alternative was to allow the class definition to be redrawn or, at least, to confine the dismissal to the remedy. The class was definable. “Consumers who purchased bottled LPG in Argentina between 1993 and 1999” is an objective and verifiable criterion. Requiring its members to be identifiable in advance is excessive for mass, low-value harm, which is precisely the scenario in which Halabi admits collective redress on access-to-justice grounds. The opinion turns the dispersion of the harm against the action, when it is its very justification. Channel heterogeneity and passing-on are merits issues. That intermediaries had different strategies does not preclude a common question: whether there was an overcharge and to what extent it was passed on. The Court of Appeals had answered it on expert evidence (full pass-on); the opinion does not refute that finding, it ignores it. The economics of quantification allow aggregate pass-on to be estimated without reconstructing each purchase. The presence of other suppliers is irrelevant to the class. That YPF was not the only wholesale supplier goes to causation and possible umbrella effects, not to the definition of the class. Outright dismissal for a defect in the remedy. If the cy-près remedy was inappropriate, the proper course was to reverse that part and require a distribution mechanism linked to the class (for instance, a reduction in the price of LPG cylinders or a fund allocated by proximity), not to dismiss the claim. No answer for the direct purchaser. The Court does not say who has standing to recover the overcharge. Excluding the indirect purchaser without securing the direct purchaser's route leaves the conduct uncompensated. The case shows that the substantive regime of Law 27,442 is not enough without procedural and evidentiary rules that make it operative. Collective standing and a class actions statute. Article 62 refers to the general law and does not provide for collective redress. It is inconsistent that consumer associations may intervene as third parties in the administrative proceedings (Art. 51) and enter into agreements with the Tribunal (Art. 28(p)), yet lack a clear judicial route. Supreme Court Rules (Acordadas) 32/2014 and 12/2016 are no substitute for a statute providing for early and appealable certification, notice and opt-out, and distribution mechanisms with subsidiary, class-linked cy-près. The standing of the Deputy Ombudsman for Competition and Consumers (Art. 86) should also be considered. Express regulation of passing-on. Article 65 already mentions “direct and indirect” purchasers, albeit only to delimit the liability of the leniency recipient. What is missing is the general rule, along the lines of Articles 12 to 14 of Directive 2014/104/EU: standing for indirect purchasers, a presumption of pass-on in their favour with the burden of proof on the defendant, and a passing-on defence against the direct purchaser. Quantification and evidence. Judicial power to estimate damages where precise proof is impossible or excessively difficult, and a presumption of harm for the cartels listed in Article 2 (Art. 17 of the Directive). In addition, a regime for access to evidence held by the infringer and in the administrative file, compatible with the ban on disclosing leniency materials (Art. 60(d)). Coordination with the ANC. The law already secures the binding effect of the final decision and summary proceedings (Art. 63), as well as the suspension of limitation (Art. 73). What is missing is a provision allowing the Tribunal to assist the civil judge on quantification, reversing the logic of the expert opinions under Article 52, and allowing its estimates of harm for setting the fine (Art. 56) to be considered in the civil action. Delay and specialisation. Twenty-four years for a judgment that does not reach the merits amounts to a denial of justice. The Specialised Chamber (Arts. 68 to 70) reviews the Tribunal's decisions, but damages actions remain before ordinary civil judges (Art. 62). Extending specialisation to these actions would bring consistency and speed. Consistency between direct and indirect purchasers. If indirect purchasers are admitted, a pass-on defence against direct purchasers is justified; if they are excluded, that defence must fall and the direct purchaser must recover the full overcharge (the Hanover Shoe–Illinois Brick pairing). The civil fine under Article 64, set by the judge in favour of the injured party, can strengthen deterrence where individual harm is small. UUC v. Repsol-YPF leaves a sanctioned infringement, a proven and quantified harm, and no compensation. The ruling is right to reject a remedy unrelated to the victims but, by deciding by referral and at the last stage, it turns the absence of procedural rules into de facto immunity for the infringer. The answer cannot be left to case-by-case adjudication. A class actions statute and express regulation of passing-on and quantification in Chapter IX of Law 27,442 (Arts. 62 to 65) are preconditions for private enforcement to move from promise to a real component of the competition system. © 2025 Wolters Kluwer N.V. and/or its subsidiaries. title: Canon's $2,499 EOS R6 V Earns Amazon's Choice With Just 19 Reviews - Y.M.Cinema Magazine
content: Canon’s video-focused EOS R6 V has received Amazon’s Choice recognition despite having only 19 customer ratings. Priced at $2,499, the full-frame mirrorless camera offers 7K RAW recording, Open Gate capture, and active cooling. Interestingly, Canon insists that despite these capabilities, the R6 V is not a Cinema EOS camera. The Canon EOS R6 V ($2,499 on Amazon) has received Amazon’s Choice designation on Amazon US, an interesting development for a relatively new video-oriented mirrorless camera. At the time of writing, the listing shows a 4.5-star customer rating based on just 19 ratings, with the camera priced at $2,499. Amazon also indicates that only three units remain in stock, with Prime delivery available the following day. However, Amazon’s Choice should not be confused with Amazon’s Best Seller designation. The badge is associated with Amazon’s product recommendation system and does not necessarily indicate exceptional sales volume. Nevertheless, receiving this recognition with such a limited number of customer ratings is noteworthy. Check out the Amazon listing. Announced in May 2026, the EOS R6 V is built around a 32.5MP full-frame CMOS sensor and Canon’s DIGIC X processor. Its video capabilities include internal 7K RAW recording at up to 60p, 7K Open Gate recording at up to 30p, oversampled 4K at up to 60p, and uncropped 4K 120p slow-motion recording. The camera also incorporates in-body image stabilization, Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS autofocus technology, and an internal cooling fan designed to support extended recording sessions. Unlike Canon’s traditional EOS R cameras, the R6 V adopts a video-oriented body without an electronic viewfinder. It also features a front recording button, dedicated vertical mounting options, and integrated zoom controls. Essentially, Canon has packed an impressive collection of advanced filmmaking features into a compact body costing substantially less than many dedicated cinema cameras. Perhaps the most intriguing aspect of the EOS R6 V is Canon’s own explanation of its positioning. In its official product FAQ, Canon explicitly states: The EOS R6 V is a Canon EOS V Series mirrorless camera, not a Cinema EOS camera. Canon describes the camera as a tool for video-first content creation, emphasizing solo creators, vloggers, and filmmakers managing their own productions. Cinema EOS cameras, according to Canon, are generally intended for professional productions involving dedicated crews, offering expanded connectivity, specialized recording workflows, and more granular manual controls. The EOS R6 V already offers acquisition capabilities associated with professional filmmaking, including 7K RAW, Open Gate, and high-frame-rate recording. Yet Canon deliberately positions it outside the Cinema EOS family. The separation is increasingly about workflow, connectivity, interface design, and production requirements rather than resolution alone. Anyway, in our opinion, the EOS R6 V demonstrates how much filmmaking technology Canon can now deliver for $2,499. Its Amazon’s Choice recognition adds a commercial dimension to that story, although sustained sales rankings will be needed to establish whether the camera becomes a genuine marketplace success. title: We Need to Super-Size Perkins V - New America
content: At New America, our work spans across five issue areas—each essential to building a nation and a world where everyone can thrive. For over 25 years, New America’s insights and policy solutions have helped usher in meaningful change. Discover recent stories of how we have turned bold ideas into real-world impact. Now is the time to double funding for this foundational community college CTE investment With a new Congress, now is the time to think big about community colleges as engines of economic opportunity. One place to start: build on a program that already works. The Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act (often called Perkins V because the law is in its fifth iteration) is the only federal funding community colleges can count on every year to invest in their own capacity, rather than funding that passes through students as financial aid. Yet many people, even some of its champions, think of Perkins V as a high school program. That blind spot has consequences: for two years running, the administration’s budget has proposed limiting Perkins V to school districts, which would end federal support for postsecondary career and technical education. Every year, colleges receive a Perkins V allocation for their career and technical programs, which tend to be the most expensive to run and often lead to good jobs. Unlike financial aid, which works like a voucher and follows students, Perkins V invests directly in the institution: the equipment, staff, and supports that make those programs work. And because the money arrives by formula every year, colleges can build lasting capacity around it. That foundation also positions colleges to win competitive grants that take more capacity to apply for and manage, such as NSF’s Advanced Technological Education program and DOL’s Strengthening Community Colleges Training Grants. The latest SCC round shows how the pieces fit together: it focuses on helping colleges build programs eligible for the new Workforce Pell Grants. Workforce Pell pays tuition, but colleges still need equipment, instructors and support services to stand those programs up. That round awarded $65 million to consortia in seven states. Competitive grants reach a handful of colleges; Perkins V reaches colleges in every state, every year. Because Perkins V flows through states, there’s no national picture of how colleges spend it. But colleges report using it for the things that make expensive programs work and that tuition aid doesn’t cover: Better data would show policymakers what this money buys. Pairing new funding with publicly available college-level reporting on spending and outcomes would allow Perkins V to prove its value as a foundational investment. The program can be invisible at colleges because it is relatively small, at about $1.4 billion a year, compared to $36 billion for Pell Grants or $3 billion for WIOA Title 1. That money is distributed across all states, and each state has discretion over how much it allocates between high schools and community colleges (ranging from 10 percent in Rhode Island to 60 percent in Colorado). College-level awards range from $50,000 (the minimum allowable grant amount) to around $4 million per year. And it has been shrinking. Adjusted for inflation, Perkins V funding is about half what it was in 1980, a point bipartisan CTE leaders in Congress have made in their annual funding requests. We can do better. At today’s state splits, doubling Perkins would double what colleges receive, without taking a dollar from high schools. That’s enough to make Perkins the anchor investment that expands college capacity and strengthens programs that lead to good jobs. The last significant investment we made in building capacity at community colleges was the $1.9 billion Trade Adjustment Assistance Community College and Career Training (TAACCT) program, which awarded competitive grants to community colleges to expand CTE programs during the 2009 recession. Rigorous research on the impact of the early TAACCT grants found that they increased CTE enrollment and completions, particularly certificates. That was a one-time competitive investment that mostly went to the colleges with the most capacity. Just imagine the impact of making an enduring, super-sized investment in formula funding for every community college through Perkins V. Perkins V is a program with rare bipartisan support, and no wonder. With the coming disruption of increased automation in the labor market, we need better hands-on training programs at community colleges. Now is the time to super-size Perkins and to make sure we can see what it builds at community colleges. title: Section V, RCSD reviewing end-of-game brawl between Monroe, East High football teams - 13WHAM-TV
content: What actions is Section V taking regarding the football game altercation? Who will East face in the Section V Class B championship game? Why is the Rochester City School District reviewing the game incident? Rochester, N.Y. — A fight between players broke out at the end of Saturday's Section V Class B football semifinal game between East/World of Inquiry and Monroe High School, with several spectators entering the playing field as officials worked to break up the fight. East won the game 14-6, handing Monroe — the reigning Class B state champion — its first loss in two years. With the win, East advanced to the Section V Class B championship game to face Honeoye Falls-Lima. Jamie Jamal Anderson's son was playing in the game. Anderson said what was supposed to be a fun time cheering has son on soon turned chaotic. "I lost track of time. I just hopped over the gate, and I had to make sure my son was safe," Anderson said. "We're all trying to make these kids get into a situation that they never had before, change their lives." Section V said it is working with the Rochester City School District to review what happened at the game, adding that the status of the upcoming championship game  "remains under review." In a statement released Sunday afternoon, the Rochester City School District said it is reviewing what happened and will handle any violations under its Code of Conduct. "We have to all come together and make everybody accountable: the coaches, the players, the community," Anderson said. As of Sunday night, Section V's website showed Honeoye Falls-Lima will play an opponent to be determined in the Class B championship game. A previous version of the scheduled listed East as the opponent.

title: Would You Rather: Cadillac Escalade IQ vs. Escalade-V - Car and Driver
content: For about $160,000, are you taking the 682-hp supercharged gas Escalade or the 750-hp electric one? A lot of companies build EV models that have an internal-combustion analogue, with the guiding principle of, “the car you liked before, but electric.” There’s a tight thematic cohesiveness to that approach—a BMW i3 and M340i each endeavor to arrive at their optimized level of BMW 3-ness despite the differing powertrains—but the Cadillac Escalade is not like that. Yes, there are gas and electric versions, but they’re similar only inasmuch as they each avidly pursue the high-level Escalade goals of cosseting bigness and cocky braggadocio. When Tony Soprano got an Escalade in season 5 of The Sopranos, the only question around that casting decision was, what took so long? Today Tony would have more choices in his pursuit of the maximum expression of GM SUV, as do any of us with about $160,000 to spend. Namely, would you rather have a supercharged V-8 Escalade-V or an electric Escalade IQ? Cadillac designed the Escalade-V’s exhaust to be extra boisterous, adding a 360-degree loop to the passenger’s-side pipe to equalize the length with the driver’s-side counterpart, for maximum sonic awesomeness. The IQ does not have equal-length dual exhaust. Whatever exhaust it does produce will get you into a tedious and possibly confrontational discussion of well-to-wheel emissions with your uncle at Thanksgiving. However, you’ll never have to worry about thieves stealing your catalytic converters, so I’ll call that one a draw. Looking at the specs, I’m surprised to see that the Escalade-V weighs eight pounds more than the IQ. Hold on, that doesn’t sound right—let me check my notes—sorry, my curb-weight figure for the Escalade-V inadvertently included a Toyota GR86 parked on its roof. Remove that extra car, and the supercharged Escalade is quite a bit lighter: 6290 pounds for the V, and a pavement-crushing 9120 pounds for the IQ. Despite the weight disparity, the two Slades are evenly matched in a drag race, with the 750-hp IQ trailing the 682-hp V by a couple tenths of a second to 60 mph (4.5 seconds to 4.3). On a rolling start from 5 mph, they’re tied at 4.7 seconds, and passing a dawdler will be a quicker task in the IQ: 50 to 70 mph in 2.6 seconds, versus 3.1 seconds for the loud Caddy. Now, I’m old enough to remember the days when a Ferrari 458 Italia felt like it had pretty decent passing power, but the Escalade IQ’s 2.1-second 30-to-50-mph time beats the Ferrari by a tenth. If the IQ had been part of our Chariots of the Gods comparison test in 2011, its 50-to-70-mph time would have slotted it a tenth of a second behind the 458 and two-tenths ahead of the McLaren MP4-12C. Neither of those, when accelerating, heave their hoods skyward like a 70-foot Viking sportfish climbing on a plane, but the Escalade IQ certainly does. And they say EVs don’t bring any drama to the experience—behind the wheel, the IQ accelerating like my favorite Ferrari of all time feels as improbable as it actually is, like the vehicle itself is struggling to cope with its superpowers. An Escalade-V drives more like a mutant CT5-V Blackwing, and it’s definitely the Escalade where the driver’s seat is more desirable than one of the chauffeur chairs in back. If we accept that one of the primary goals for an Escalade is to project brash confidence, and that hugeness is fundamental to that project, the Escalade IQ wins going away. It reminds me of a scaled-up Rolls-Royce Cullinan in the side profile, and there’s a lot of side to behold: the IQ is more than a foot longer than the gas-powered Escalade. It’s also just newer, and I think it helps the premium aura not to have a bunch of Chevys and GMCs out there copping your style with very similar bodies. Also: rear-axle steering is unequivocally a flex, and the internal-combustion Escalade doesn’t have it. Inside, both Escalades offer huge screens, lots of leather, and power-operated doors. However, only the IQ is eligible for the Curated by Cadillac program, wherein buyers fork over an additional $54,995 and get to choose from a huge palette of colors, inside and out. With 44 interior color choices, you can certainly spec a one-of-one IQ, while the Escalade-V sticks with “Yukon Denali, but fancier” as a guiding principle. Advantage, IQ. When we’re discussing EVs versus internal combustion, range is usually an easy win for the gas-powered candidate. But not here—the Escalade-V has an EPA-rated 312 miles of range, while the IQ gets a 465-mile rating. Yes, the V will refuel a lot quicker, but you’ll be stopping way more often. And if your gas pump stops at $100, you might technically need to fill twice to top off the 24-gallon tank with premium. Another factor I have to consider is rap music references, and on that front the Escalade-V is the easy winner, if only because the IQ is too new—most Escalade lyrics concern gas-powered models by default. Cadillac did hire Big Boi from Outkast to rap about the IQ, but that doesn’t count. (“Escalade IQ, this is the intro to, the all-electric Cadillac perfection ...”) I’m sure we’ll get there eventually: “Rolling in the IQ to the house with a view, IQ got the roof see-through, park the IQ next to the other ’cause I just bought two.” Finally, I think part of the Escalade mystique has always hinged on leadership. This is a boss truck, from Sopranos to Succession. And where are the luxury winds blowing? It seems to me that in this space, which is to say “not a V-12 Ferrari,” the market is amenable to electrification and the technology is progressing fast. GM just announced that its forthcoming battery chemistry will improve range while being 20 percent more compact. There will come a time, maybe not far off, when EVs just make more sense objectively (they already do, depending on use case) and internal combustion will be the nostalgia play. So in this Would You Rather, I’m embracing that future and going for the Escalade IQ. The V is charming, but for $160,000, the IQ better fulfills the role of flagship SUV—quick, cocky, luxurious, and incontrovertibly baller. Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.
